extracted.intended_audience: students/readers of arithmetic and classical geometry (learners of rules of proportion)
extracted.subtask_description: A historical treatise excerpt listing operational rules and properties of proportions: how to add, subtract, multiply proportions; how to interpose mean terms; distinctions between arithmetic and geometric proportionality; invariance under multiplication/division; and behavior under augmentation and diminution of extremes.

rubrics_metrics.name: De additione proportionum ad invicem
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules for adding proportions to one another ("De addinone proportionum ad inuicem").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the proportions comparable by placing them in like terms (i.e., reduce to common denominators by multiplying denominators/terms as needed), then form the sum; the resulting proportion is obtained by summing the corresponding numerators after bringing to common denominators. Examples and worked computations are given; attention is called to arranging the proportions so that corresponding terms align before adding.

rubrics_metrics.name: De subtractione proportionum ab invicem
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules for subtracting one proportion from another ("fubtraotione proportionum ab inuicem").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write the two proportions with corresponding terms (put the proportion to be subtracted and the one from which to subtract in comparable terms), convert to common denominators by multiplying appropriate terms, then subtract the corresponding terms to obtain the difference-proportion. Several worked examples show choosing convenient terms to simplify operations and notes that one must ensure correct relative placement (which term is to be subtracted from which).

rubrics_metrics.name: De multiplicarione proportionum
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To multiply proportions, multiply the respective denominators (and numerators) so that the denominator of the product is the product of denominators of the factors; products of proportions yield double, triple, quadruple (etc.) proportions according to how many factors and by which factors they are multiplied. The text gives numerical examples illustrating how multiplying one proportion by another yields composite proportional relations (e.g., double × triple → sextuple), and notes that repeated multiplication among proportions produces a continuous proportionality among the resulting products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportiones continuae / compositio proportionum
rubrics_metrics.description: Composition and continuous chaining of proportions (proportiones inter se; continuous proportions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A proportion may be divided into multiple proportions by interposing terms: inserting one or more means between extremes turns one proportion into several continuous proportions. The composition of several proportions into a chain is treated: how to recognize when several proportions form a continuous proportional series and how to compose/decompose such chains. Examples demonstrate how inserting one term can make a proportion into a dupla, tripla, quadrupla, etc., and how to recover unknown terms by using the chain rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interponere termini (insertion of intermediate terms)
rubrics_metrics.description: How to interpolate one or more terms between extremes to form desired proportional relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To find an intermediate term that makes given extremes relate as a particular multiple (double, triple, quadruple, etc.), insert a term between the extremes and use the known proportions to determine its value. The method: choose convenient known terms, set up the proportion(s) with the interposed term(s), and solve by the usual proportion rules. Worked examples show interpolation to obtain, e.g., tripla, ferquitertia, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversion to common denomination when manipulating proportions
rubrics_metrics.description: When performing operations (addition, subtraction, comparison) on proportions, convert them to a common 'denominator' by multiplying terms appropriately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frequently one makes denominators (or corresponding positions) common by multiplying numerators/denominators of proportions by suitable factors; the product of denominators becomes the denominator of the compound proportion. The text repeatedly uses this technique in examples for adding, subtracting, and comparing proportions and warns to choose convenient factors to simplify calculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportio aritbmetica (arithmetic proportionality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition and properties of arithmetic proportionality: proportions in which increments (augmentations) are equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arithmetic proportionality is preserved when equal arithmetic increments are applied to corresponding terms: adding the same quantity to both extremes preserves the arithmetic proportional relationship appropriately described. The treatise gives examples of arithmetic proportions (fractions like 4:6:8 etc.) and shows how augmentation or diminution by units affects the arithmetic proportionality. It contrasts arithmetic proportion with geometric proportion and notes when arithmetic proportionality is maintained or altered by operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportio geometrica (geometric proportionality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition and properties of geometric proportionality: proportions in which terms are in multiplicative relation (multiples/factors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric proportionality is preserved by multiplying corresponding terms by the same factor; doubling, tripling, quadrupling terms yields corresponding double/triple/quadruple proportional relations. The text shows examples (dupla, tripla, quadrupla) and explains how multiplying extremes preserves the geometric proportionality and how geometric relations compose under multiplication of factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invariance of proportion under multiplication/division by same factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiplying or dividing both terms of a proportion by the same number preserves the proportional relation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you multiply (or divide) both terms of a proportion by the same quantity, the resulting proportion is equivalent; this is used repeatedly to make convenient forms for addition/subtraction or to combine proportions. Numerical examples illustrate converting to equivalent proportions by uniform multiplication/division of terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of augmenting or diminishing extremes on proportions
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules describing how adding or subtracting quantities to extremes affects the resulting proportion (augmentation/augmentation of extremes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adding the same quantity to both extremes tends to produce arithmetic effects (proportio arithmetica), while multiplicative changes (scaling) produce geometric effects. The text gives concrete numeric examples showing when an added term increases the larger extreme and how the proportion changes, including special cases and cautions (e.g., one must watch relative sizes and denominators when performing these operations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Formation of multiple proportions (dupla, tripla, quadrupla, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: How to form and interpret double, triple, quadruple (and higher) proportions by combining or multiplying proportions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise shows that composing proportions yields named multiplicative relations: a dupla (double), tripla (triple), quadrupla, ferquiquarta, etc., and gives arithmetic examples (e.g., how a dupla combined with a tripla yields a sextuple relation). Guidance includes how to compute the combined denominators/numerators and how to reason about the resulting proportionality (how many times greater, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintaining proportional equality across chains
rubrics_metrics.description: If proportions are similar/continuous then relations of equality/inequality propagate across the chain of proportions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes that if two proportions are equimultiples or correspond in a chain (continuous proportions), then equality or relative magnitude (greater/less) can be deduced for other linked terms; it gives principle-level guidance for reasoning about whole chains rather than isolated pairs and includes examples of deducing magnitudes from combined proportional relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical procedures and examples for calculation
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent emphasis on practical calculation techniques (choose convenient terms, multiply to common denominators, insert handy intermediate terms) and many numerical examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise repeatedly advises using convenient numeric choices, multiplying to obtain common denominators, and working through concrete numeric examples (e.g., 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, etc.) to internalize rules. It warns about pitfalls when choosing terms and shows step-by-step examples for addition, subtraction, multiplication, interpolation, and conversion between arithmetic and geometric proportionalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction and interplay between arithmetic and geometric proportionalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicit comparison of arithmetic vs geometric proportion: when each concept applies and how operations affect each.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text contrasts the two: arithmetic proportionality concerns equal additive increments; geometric proportionality concerns multiplicative scaling. It gives rules showing that some operations (adding equal quantities) preserve arithmetic proportionality, while others (multiplying by the same factor) preserve geometric proportionality, and discusses mixed situations and conversion principles with examples.
